lesson.title: AWS EC2: instance types credits and purchasing
lesson.why: A low hourly instance price can hide CPU throttling, memory pressure, or surplus-credit charges. Choosing compute requires a workload profile rather than a familiar instance name.
lesson.what: Separate processor architecture, resource ratios, burst accounting, and purchasing contracts. Evaluate a hypothetical worker without launching infrastructure or assuming a particular regional price.

concepts.name: Match the limiting resource
concepts.body: General purpose, compute optimized, and memory optimized families offer different ratios. CPU utilization alone misses memory, storage throughput, and network ceilings. An Arm instance also requires compatible binaries and images; a cheaper architecture is not a transparent replacement for every application.

concepts.name: Understand credit accounting
concepts.body: One CPU credit represents one vCPU running at full utilization for one minute. Burstable instances earn credits at a size-specific baseline. Standard mode gradually returns toward baseline when credits run out; Unlimited can continue above baseline using surplus credits that may become billable.

concepts.name: Separate price from capacity
concepts.body: On-Demand avoids a usage commitment. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances offer contractual discounts with different flexibility; a discount is not generally a capacity reservation. Spot uses spare capacity and can be interrupted, so checkpointing and replacement capacity belong in the design.

concepts.name: Measure a representative window
concepts.body: Compare latency, CPUCreditBalance, surplus-credit metrics, memory, and disk queues through peak periods. Unlimited accounting uses a rolling 24-hour window or shorter instance lifetime. Sustained high CPU may favor a nonburstable family even when its listed hourly price is higher.

e2e: Record request rate, latency objective, memory working set, and processor compatibility.
Translate peak demand into required vCPU capacity and storage throughput.
Calculate credit consumption for the proposed burstable size before comparing prices.
Choose a purchase model compatible with interruption tolerance and stable demand.
Benchmark later in an approved environment; compare total cost and tail latency before migration.

tasks.name: Classify a worker
tasks.goal: Identify a plausible family from evidence.
steps: Offline, compare a worker using 90% CPU and 20% memory with one using 25% CPU and 95% memory.
Recommend compute optimized for investigation in the first case and memory optimized in the second; list disk latency as an unresolved measurement.

tasks.name: Calculate credit depletion
steps: Assume two vCPUs, 20% baseline per vCPU, 50% average utilization, and 72 starting credits.
Earning is 2 x 0.20 x 60 = 24 credits/hour; spending is 60. Net depletion is 36/hour, so the balance lasts two hours. This is an illustrative model, not a quoted instance specification.

tasks.name: Compare interruption choices
steps: A batch job checkpoints every five minutes; an interactive database cannot tolerate replacement interruptions.
Assign Spot only as a candidate for the checkpointed worker. Include checkpoint storage, retry work, and an On-Demand fallback rather than asserting guaranteed savings.

tasks.name: Define a rollout gate
steps: Draft acceptance criteria: unchanged error rate, p95 latency within its objective, and no memory exhaustion during a representative peak.
Describe rollback to the previous image and size. The offline calculations do not establish real cloud performance or capacity availability.

key_terms: vCPU: a virtual processor allocation.
Baseline: sustainable CPU level associated with credit earning.
Surplus credit: above-balance CPU consumption in Unlimited mode.
Spot: interruptible spare-capacity purchasing.
Working set: memory actively needed by a workload.
lesson.safety: Use paper calculations only. Real experiments can incur instance, volume, address, transfer, and Unlimited credit charges; Free Tier eligibility must never be assumed.
cleanup: Retain the assumptions and discard scratch calculations when finished.
No resources were created; a future benchmark needs explicit termination and volume-retention checks.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a cheap burstable worker becomes slow every afternoon. How would you distinguish throttling from a purchasing mistake?
interview_points: Correlate credit balance and CPU with latency, memory, and disk queues.
Check Standard versus Unlimited and surplus-credit charges.
Compare a representative nonburstable alternative rather than assuming a discount fixes resource limits.

aws-core/aws-ec2-instance-types-credits-.core: EC2 sizing and purchasing are separate decisions. Standard credit depletion constrains sustained CPU; Unlimited can add charges. Measure the bottleneck, check architecture compatibility, and compare total cost including retries and attached resources.

storyboard.title: A burstable worker exhausts its balance
storyboard.objective: Connect CPU demand to credit depletion and a safer sizing decision.

scenes.title: Short burst
scenes.caption: Earned credits cover temporary excess CPU.
scenes.narration: The worker briefly exceeds baseline, consuming accumulated credits while meeting its latency objective.

scenes.title: Sustained demand
scenes.caption: Standard mode cannot sustain the same burst indefinitely.
scenes.narration: Continuous demand drains the balance. Standard mode trends toward baseline; Unlimited instead introduces possible surplus charges.

scenes.title: Choose measured capacity
scenes.caption: Revisit the family instead of hiding the symptom.
scenes.narration: The planner compares nonburstable capacity using representative measurements, then defines a reversible migration rather than promising savings.

lesson.title: AWS EC2: Auto Scaling and High Availability
lesson.why: Replacing an instance is not the same as keeping an application available. Scaling decisions must account for startup delays, usable capacity, and correlated Availability Zone failures.
lesson.what: Design an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer using explicit minimum capacity, meaningful health checks, and a tested launch template. Model failure offline before provisioning.

concepts.name: Desired capacity is a target
concepts.body: An Auto Scaling group reconciles actual membership toward desired capacity within minimum and maximum limits. Launch failures, quotas, and unavailable capacity can prevent immediate convergence. Multiple subnets distribute instances across zones, but the surviving zones still need sufficient usable capacity.

concepts.name: Health has multiple meanings
concepts.body: EC2 checks primarily identify instance and infrastructure problems. Load balancer health checks identify application reachability and must be enabled for the group to use them in replacement decisions. A process that returns errors may pass infrastructure checks indefinitely.

concepts.name: Scaling is delayed feedback
concepts.body: Target tracking changes capacity from a utilization metric. Instance warmup prevents immature capacity from distorting decisions; health-check grace periods prevent premature replacement during startup. Neither makes slow initialization disappear. Request backlog can grow while new instances prepare.

concepts.name: Availability includes state
concepts.body: Store durable data outside replaceable instances and avoid dependence on one node's session memory. Lifecycle hooks can coordinate initialization or draining, with bounded timeouts. Deployments need healthy replacement capacity before old instances leave; maximum size and database limits constrain this overlap.

e2e: Create a versioned launch-template proposal with deterministic bootstrap and external state.
Spread desired capacity across at least two zones and calculate one-zone-loss headroom.
Register instances with a target group and define application-level health criteria.
Apply scaling targets while allowing measured startup and warmup time.
Simulate failure, verify surviving throughput, and revise capacity or initialization assumptions.

tasks.name: Draw the failure domain
tasks.goal: Distinguish redundant instances from redundant zones.
steps: Sketch four instances, two in each zone, behind one regional load balancer.
Mark the database and session store. Explain why four instances in one zone would not survive that zone's outage.

tasks.name: Calculate surviving capacity
tasks.goal: Work out an explicit offline capacity bound.
steps: Assume each healthy instance handles 80 requests/second at the latency objective and demand is 240.
Four instances provide 320, but losing one of two equally populated zones leaves 160. Six instances, three per zone, leave 240; this has no extra post-failure headroom.

tasks.name: Trace a bad deployment
steps: Given EC2 status healthy and target health failing with HTTP 500, identify application startup or dependency failure as a hypothesis.
Explain that target-health removal does not itself guarantee group replacement unless the group's corresponding health checks are enabled.

tasks.name: Plan recovery and rollback
steps: Write a rollout sequence that canaries a new launch-template version, waits for readiness, and retains the previous version.
Specify rollback on rising errors. These paper simulations do not prove bootstrap, IAM permissions, or real failover timing.

key_terms: Desired capacity: membership count the group seeks.
Warmup: period before new capacity fully participates in scaling calculations.
Grace period: initial interval protecting startup from certain health replacements.
Lifecycle hook: bounded pause in an instance transition.
Headroom: capacity beyond current required load.
lesson.safety: Do not create a group. Real minimum, maximum, and overlapping deployment capacity affect spend; quotas and budgets are guardrails, not application availability guarantees.
cleanup: Keep the topology and arithmetic as review evidence.
For future approved tests, remove groups and load balancers and check retained volumes and logs.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a two-zone service has four healthy instances but fails during a zone outage. What would you investigate?
interview_points: Calculate surviving capacity rather than counting replicas.
Inspect application health and startup time.
Find shared state or dependencies in the failed zone.
Check quotas, launch failures, and rollback readiness.

aws-core/aws-ec2-auto-scaling-and-high-a.core: Auto Scaling restores desired capacity, not instantaneous availability. Combine zone diversity, failure headroom, application health, measured warmup, and external state. Replacement must not become a loop caused by broken bootstrap.

storyboard.title: An Auto Scaling group loses a zone
storyboard.objective: Show why replacement needs time and surviving capacity.

scenes.title: Serve with headroom
scenes.caption: Healthy targets share requests across zones.
scenes.narration: The load balancer sends traffic to ready instances while the group maintains the chosen desired capacity.

scenes.title: Zone capacity disappears
scenes.caption: Routing changes before replacement finishes.
scenes.narration: Losing a zone removes usable targets. Surviving instances must handle demand during detection, launch, and application startup.

scenes.title: Restore usable capacity
scenes.caption: Only ready replacements improve throughput.
scenes.narration: The group launches replacements and health checks admit them after initialization; engineers verify latency before declaring recovery.

lesson.title: AWS IAM: roles policies and permission evaluation
lesson.why: An Allow statement does not by itself establish access. Troubleshooting IAM requires the actual principal, resource, action, request context, and all applicable policy layers.
lesson.what: Evaluate small hypothetical requests while separating authentication, role trust, permission grants, limiting policies, and service-specific resource rules. Never test by widening a production policy.

concepts.name: Trust and permissions differ
concepts.body: A role trust policy identifies who may assume the role, subject to conditions and the caller's authorization. The role's permission policies govern subsequent service requests. Temporary credentials reduce long-lived secret exposure but do not automatically make a broad role least privileged.

concepts.name: Deny and implicit denial
concepts.body: Applicable explicit denies override allows. Absent a required allow, access is implicitly denied. Identity and resource policies can combine for same-account access, but the precise principal named matters. Cross-account access generally requires authorization on both sides, with service-specific exceptions and additional controls.

concepts.name: Boundaries are not grants
concepts.body: Permissions boundaries, session policies, and Organizations controls can limit permissions; attaching one does not grant actions. Resource-policy grants directly to a same-account user or role session have evaluation nuances, so an intersection-only diagram is not a complete universal IAM algorithm.

concepts.name: Context makes policies concrete
concepts.body: Actions require correctly scoped resource ARNs and supported conditions. Bucket listing and object reading target different resource types. KMS key policy, VPC endpoint policy, organization controls, and encryption context may also matter. A policy simulator is useful evidence, not proof of every live service interaction.

e2e: Identify the caller ARN and whether it represents a user, role, or assumed-role session.
Record the exact service action, resource ARN, account relationship, and condition context.
Check applicable explicit denies before searching for a missing allow.
Evaluate grants and limits with the correct principal-specific and service-specific rules.
Propose the narrowest change and an approved positive and negative verification plan.

tasks.name: Separate two requests
tasks.goal: Distinguish assuming a role from using it.
steps: Draw a deployment identity requesting sts:AssumeRole, then its session requesting s3:GetObject.
Assign role trust to the first request and object authorization to the second. Explain why editing trust alone cannot grant object reads.

tasks.name: Work a bounded decision table
steps: Assume identity-only same-account access, no resource policy, an identity Allow for GetObject, a boundary allowing only GetObject, and an SCP explicitly denying DeleteObject.
Expected outcomes: GetObject may proceed if other required controls allow it; DeleteObject is denied; PutObject lacks an allow. List these assumptions beside the table.

tasks.name: Correct resource scope
steps: On paper, map s3:ListBucket to arn:aws:s3:::example-training and s3:GetObject to arn:aws:s3:::example-training/reports/*.
Add a requirement that only the reports prefix may be listed; note that the supported prefix condition belongs to the listing request.

tasks.name: Challenge the simplified model
steps: Change the example to a resource policy granting an assumed-role session directly and flag the need for principal-specific evaluation.
Do not claim the earlier table proves this request. Draft a negative test for another prefix without issuing cloud commands.

key_terms: Principal: authenticated identity making a request.
Trust policy: role-assumption authorization policy.
Boundary: maximum identity permission scope, not a grant.
Explicit deny: matching prohibition that overrides allows.
Session policy: additional limit applied to temporary sessions.
lesson.safety: Use fictional ARNs and no credentials. Offline tables do not prove live IAM behavior; never add wildcard administration to diagnose access, and account for audit-log costs in future tests.
cleanup: Discard hypothetical policies rather than applying them.
Keep the request assumptions and expected denials for review.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a role has AdministratorAccess but cannot decrypt one object. How would you investigate without broadening permissions?
interview_points: Identify the actual role session and exact failed action.
Check explicit denies, boundaries, session and organization controls.
Inspect object access, KMS key policy, and request conditions.
Use bounded tests and preserve negative cases.

aws-core/aws-iam-roles-policies-and-perm.core: Evaluate IAM for a specific request, not a policy in isolation. Trust authorizes assumption; permission policies authorize actions. Explicit denies win, boundaries do not grant, and resource-principal and cross-account nuances prevent a universal intersection shortcut.

storyboard.title: A role session encounters a permission limit
storyboard.objective: Separate role assumption from authorization of an object request.

scenes.title: Assumption succeeds
scenes.caption: Trust creates a session, not unlimited access.
scenes.narration: The deployment identity satisfies the role's assumption requirements and receives temporary credentials for a distinct session.

scenes.title: Read is denied
scenes.caption: An applicable deny still overrides an allow.
scenes.narration: The session requests an object, but a matching explicit deny blocks that action despite a broad identity grant.

scenes.title: Review the actual request
scenes.caption: Repair only the justified scope.
scenes.narration: The owner reviews the denial context and proposes a narrowly authorized change with positive and negative tests.

lesson.title: AWS VPC: subnets routing endpoints and NAT
lesson.why: A route, a firewall permission, and a name lookup solve different problems. Confusing them creates unreachable private workloads or unnecessarily expensive internet paths.
lesson.what: Trace packets through a VPC using subnet associations, longest-prefix routing, endpoint choices, and return paths. All exercises use fictional addresses and offline route tables.

concepts.name: Subnets inherit a route table
concepts.body: A subnet belongs to one Availability Zone and uses an explicitly associated route table or the main table. Routing chooses a matching destination, generally the most specific prefix. A public subnet has a direct route to an internet gateway; an IPv4 instance also needs suitable addressing and security rules.

concepts.name: NAT is outbound translation
concepts.body: A public NAT gateway allows private IPv4 clients to initiate internet connections when the surrounding routes are correct. It is not a listener that grants unsolicited inbound access. NAT gateways are zonal; cross-zone routing introduces dependency and potentially transfer charges as well as processing charges.

concepts.name: Endpoints change the path
concepts.body: Gateway endpoints provide route-table paths for supported services such as S3 and DynamoDB. Interface endpoints use private network interfaces and usually private DNS for supported service APIs. Endpoint policies constrain supported access but do not replace identity or resource authorization.

concepts.name: Reachability needs every layer
concepts.body: Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless and may need explicit return-traffic rules. DNS can resolve a public address even when the intended private endpoint exists. Inspect effective routes, resolver behavior, security controls, and service authorization separately rather than adding broad rules.

e2e: Locate the source subnet, associated route table, and destination address returned by DNS.
Select the most specific applicable route and identify its target.
Trace the next hop through an endpoint, NAT gateway, or internet gateway.
Check security-group and network-ACL treatment of both request and response.
Evaluate service authorization after network reachability, then document the least-cost appropriate path.

tasks.name: Classify subnet paths
tasks.goal: Separate public addressing from route intent.
steps: Draw an application subnet with 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT and a NAT subnet with 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway.
Explain why the application is not directly internet-reachable merely because it can download updates.

tasks.name: Perform route selection
steps: Use routes 10.0.0.0/16 local, 10.2.0.0/16 peering, and 0.0.0.0/0 NAT.
For destinations 10.0.4.9, 10.2.8.7, and 203.0.113.10, expected targets are local, peering, and NAT respectively. The documentation-range address is only a label, not a connection target.

tasks.name: Remove an unnecessary hop
steps: A private worker transfers S3 data through NAT. Sketch a gateway-endpoint alternative and list route-table association, endpoint policy, bucket policy, and IAM checks.
Do not assume every AWS API supports gateway endpoints or that an endpoint grants data access.

tasks.name: Diagnose the return path
steps: Given successful DNS and a permitted outbound SYN but no response, inspect the route back and stateless ACL ephemeral-port rules.
Record one observation per layer. This paper model does not prove packet delivery, endpoint DNS, or cloud permissions.

key_terms: CIDR: network prefix expressed with a bit length.
Longest prefix: most specific matching destination.
NAT: translation of source addressing for outbound connections.
Gateway endpoint: service route-table integration.
Interface endpoint: private interface exposing a supported service.
lesson.safety: No network changes or probes are required. Actual NAT, interface endpoints, public addresses, and transferred bytes may incur charges; do not open inbound administration from the internet.
cleanup: Delete only local scratch diagrams; no cloud resources require cleanup.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, private instances reach public websites but time out against an intended private service endpoint. What do you inspect?
interview_points: Resolve the actual destination and verify private DNS.
Check subnet routes and endpoint interface security groups.
Inspect ACL return traffic and service authorization separately.
Avoid treating NAT as the universal fix.

aws-core/aws-vpc-subnets-routing-endpoin.core: Trace DNS, route selection, next hop, return traffic, and authorization separately. Public subnet routing does not itself publish an instance. NAT is outbound translation; endpoints can provide service-specific private paths without granting permissions.

storyboard.title: An S3 request takes the wrong VPC path
storyboard.objective: Explain how route choice affects reachability and cost.

scenes.title: Default path
scenes.caption: The worker reaches S3 through NAT.
scenes.narration: Without a service-specific endpoint route, matching public destinations follow the subnet's default path through NAT.

scenes.title: NAT path fails
scenes.caption: A shared network dependency blocks transfers.
scenes.narration: A failure on the NAT path stops the transfer even though the S3 service itself remains available.

scenes.title: Review a private service route
scenes.caption: Endpoint routing still requires authorization.
scenes.narration: An approved gateway endpoint provides a direct supported service path; identity, endpoint, and bucket policies still decide access.

lesson.title: AWS Lambda: invocation concurrency and retries
lesson.why: Retries can turn one event into repeated side effects, while concurrency can overwhelm a downstream database. The invocation source determines where failures are retained and retried.
lesson.what: Model synchronous calls, asynchronous delivery, and event-source polling separately. Use idempotency and bounded concurrency instead of assuming serverless means unlimited throughput or exactly-once processing.

concepts.name: Synchronous callers own retry decisions
concepts.body: A synchronous invocation returns a response or error to its caller. Lambda does not automatically rerun a function error for that direct request. Clients and integrating services may retry according to their own behavior, so a timeout does not establish that no side effect occurred.

concepts.name: Asynchronous invocation queues events
concepts.body: For asynchronous function errors, Lambda retries twice by default, with configurable error-retry and event-age controls. Throttling and system-error handling differ from function-error retries. Failure destinations or dead-letter queues preserve information, but consumers still need deduplication and an operational replay process.

concepts.name: Polling follows source semantics
concepts.body: Event source mappings poll queues or streams and invoke functions in batches. SQS visibility timeout and redrive settings shape reprocessing; partial batch responses can avoid repeating successful records. Stream failures can hold back a shard, subject to configured retry, age, and failure-handling options.

concepts.name: Concurrency is active work
concepts.body: Approximate concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by average execution duration in seconds. Reserved concurrency reserves and caps a function's share; provisioned concurrency prepares execution environments to reduce initialization latency. Neither removes downstream connection limits, and retries increase effective arrival rate.

e2e: Identify whether the event arrives synchronously, asynchronously, or through a polling mapping.
Choose a stable business idempotency key before performing an external side effect.
Set processing timeout, source retry controls, and failure retention consistently.
Bound concurrency to protect downstream systems and observe queue age or iterator age.
Replay failures only after fixing the cause and preserving duplicate protection.

tasks.name: Assign retry ownership
steps: Create columns for direct invocation, asynchronous function error, and SQS polling.
Expected owners are caller retry policy, Lambda asynchronous policy, and queue visibility/redrive plus mapping behavior. Do not apply the asynchronous two-retry default to all three.

tasks.name: Calculate active executions
steps: Assume 120 events/second and 0.25-second average duration without retries: 120 x 0.25 = 30 concurrent executions on average.
If duration becomes one second, the estimate becomes 120. Explain that bursts, tail duration, and retries require additional analysis rather than a guaranteed capacity value.

tasks.name: Handle a mixed batch
steps: Use records A, B, C with only B failing; identify the failed-record response needed when partial batch reporting is enabled for a compatible mapping.
Describe a durable idempotency record for A and C, because duplicates remain possible despite partial responses.

tasks.name: Design controlled replay
steps: A dead-letter collection contains 500 orders after a database outage. Propose capped replay, duplicate checks, and a stop condition based on database errors.
This offline design does not test real source retries, IAM permissions, or Lambda timing.

key_terms: Concurrency: executions active at the same time.
Idempotency key: identifier making repeated processing logically equivalent.
Visibility timeout: queue interval hiding an in-flight message.
Event source mapping: poller connecting a source to Lambda.
Failure destination: configured location for invocation outcome records.
lesson.safety: Do not invoke functions or create queues. Actual requests, duration, logs, provisioned concurrency, and downstream retries can cost money; never replay real payment events casually.
cleanup: Discard synthetic order identifiers; no deployed resources were used.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, one failed SQS batch causes duplicate orders. How would you prevent repeated business effects?
interview_points: Confirm queue and event-source mapping behavior.
Use stable keys and durable idempotent state transitions.
Consider partial batch failures and visibility settings.
Cap replay and monitor age, errors, and downstream saturation.

aws-core/aws-lambda-invocation-concurren.core: Retry behavior belongs to the invocation path. Direct callers decide retries; asynchronous function errors default to two retries; polling follows queue or stream controls. Concurrency is arrival rate times duration, and duplicates require business-level idempotency.

storyboard.title: A queued order is retried safely
storyboard.objective: Connect visibility, failure, and idempotent recovery.

scenes.title: Process an order
scenes.caption: The poller delivers a temporarily hidden message.
scenes.narration: Lambda receives an SQS batch and uses the order identifier to guard its durable business update.

scenes.title: Response is lost
scenes.caption: A successful side effect can still be retried.
scenes.narration: Processing stops before successful acknowledgement. Visibility eventually expires, allowing another delivery even if an order update already happened.

scenes.title: Detect the duplicate
scenes.caption: Idempotency prevents another logical order.
scenes.narration: The retry checks durable order state, recognizes the completed operation, and finishes without repeating the business effect.

lesson.title: AWS Elastic Load Balancing and target health
lesson.why: A running backend can still be unusable, and an aggressive probe can remove every backend during a dependency incident. Load-balancer health must reflect safe routing decisions.
lesson.what: Compare Application and Network Load Balancers, then trace listener rules, target groups, health transitions, and connection draining using an offline request timeline.

concepts.name: Choose the forwarding layer
concepts.body: An Application Load Balancer routes HTTP-aware traffic using listener rules such as host and path matching. A Network Load Balancer serves transport-layer use cases. Protocol, TLS termination, client identity requirements, and target type influence selection; they are not interchangeable solely on throughput.

concepts.name: Health is an observed signal
concepts.body: A target group defines probe protocol, port, path, thresholds, and expected responses. Probe success is separate from user-request success. Authentication redirects or an incorrect health path can mark useful targets unhealthy; shallow checks can conversely hide broken application dependencies.

concepts.name: All-unhealthy has special behavior
concepts.body: For an ALB target group containing only unhealthy registered targets, the load balancer fails open and routes to those targets rather than promising zero traffic. Therefore health checks are not an authorization barrier and cannot guarantee isolation of a faulty service.

concepts.name: Removal must drain work
concepts.body: Deregistration delay gives existing requests time to complete while a target leaves service. Applications need graceful shutdown and compatible request timeouts. Sticky sessions and long connections can skew load, so inspect per-target errors and latency rather than only the fleet average.

e2e: Select the load-balancer type and listener protocol from actual client requirements.
Map listener rules to target groups and verify target port and enabled zones.
Define probes that represent readiness without exposing credentials or mutating data.
Observe healthy-to-unhealthy transitions and distinguish probe failure from application errors.
Drain departing targets and verify recovery with user-facing success and latency measurements.

tasks.name: Map two listeners
steps: A browser API needs /images and /orders routing; a custom TCP protocol needs transport forwarding.
Choose ALB for the HTTP rule requirement and investigate NLB for the TCP service. List TLS termination location as an explicit remaining decision.

tasks.name: Work a probe timeline
tasks.goal: Calculate detection without a false guarantee.
steps: Assume a simplified probe every ten seconds and an unhealthy threshold of three. A failure immediately after a success yields failures near seconds 10, 20, and 30.
Expected modeled detection is about 30 seconds, not instant. Actual distributed checks, timeouts, and scheduling mean this is not a promised service timing.

tasks.name: Diagnose an all-red group
steps: Every ALB target returns 503 from /ready because a shared dependency is unavailable.
Explain fail-open behavior for an all-unhealthy registered group. Propose incident mitigation at the application or traffic-management layer rather than treating health checks as a firewall.

tasks.name: Plan graceful replacement
steps: For a synthetic request lasting 25 seconds, compare immediate process termination with a drain period that covers the request and shutdown margin.
Write a sequence: stop admitting work, deregister, finish bounded work, terminate. This model does not validate real connection or cloud behavior.

key_terms: Listener: entry point receiving traffic on a protocol and port.
Target group: backend collection with routing and health settings.
Readiness: ability to accept useful work now.
Fail-open: routing despite failed health when all registered targets are unhealthy.
Deregistration delay: time allowed for draining.
lesson.safety: Keep exercises offline. Load balancers, capacity units, addresses, logs, and transfer can incur charges. Health endpoints must not disclose secrets or perform writes.
cleanup: Retain the routing and drain sequence.
Remove scratch timelines; no listeners or targets were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, requests still reach an ALB target group when every target is unhealthy. Is that proof health checks are broken?
interview_points: Explain documented all-unhealthy fail-open behavior.
Inspect probe configuration and shared dependencies.
Use application safeguards rather than probes as access control.
Plan controlled recovery and measure user-facing outcomes.

aws-core/aws-elastic-load-balancing-and-.core: ELB health determines routing evidence, not authorization or perfect availability. Choose the correct forwarding layer, make readiness meaningful, understand ALB all-unhealthy fail-open behavior, and drain long-running work during replacement.

storyboard.title: ALB health fails across a target group
storyboard.objective: Explain health routing and its all-unhealthy exception.

scenes.title: Healthy routing
scenes.caption: Requests use healthy registered targets.
scenes.narration: The listener selects a target group and sends the request to a backend currently passing its health checks.

scenes.title: Every probe fails
scenes.caption: ALB may fail open to unhealthy targets.
scenes.narration: A common dependency breaks every probe. With only unhealthy registered targets, the group does not become an access-control barrier.

scenes.title: Restore readiness carefully
scenes.caption: Check useful requests, not only green probes.
scenes.narration: Operators repair the dependency and verify both probe recovery and representative user requests before ending mitigation.

lesson.title: AWS Organizations Control Tower and SCPs
lesson.why: Account sprawl makes inconsistent access and logging hard to detect. Organization-wide guardrails reduce repeated configuration work, but a mistaken deny can also block legitimate operations broadly.
lesson.what: Design a small multi-account hierarchy with separate billing, governance, and workload responsibilities. Use SCPs as permission limits and Control Tower as a landing-zone governance service.

concepts.name: Accounts form isolation boundaries
concepts.body: Organizations groups member accounts into organizational units under a root. Accounts separate many quotas, billing attribution, and administrative boundaries. Organize OUs around policy needs and operational lifecycle rather than copying a changing company organization chart mechanically.

concepts.name: SCPs constrain rather than authorize
concepts.body: A service control policy sets maximum permissions for affected member-account principals; it grants nothing by itself. Applicable explicit denies win. Allow-list strategies require allowed actions through the hierarchy, so an omitted ancestor allow can block a child despite a local identity grant.

concepts.name: Scope has important exceptions
concepts.body: SCPs do not restrict principals in the management account and do not affect service-linked roles. They are not a universal resource firewall against every external principal. Resource policies and other applicable organization controls require separate evaluation, making a dedicated management account especially important.

concepts.name: Landing zones need operations
concepts.body: Control Tower helps establish and govern a multi-account landing zone using controls and account provisioning workflows. Preventive and detective controls differ: detecting drift does not necessarily block it. Baselines still need owners, exception handling, evidence retention, and controlled updates.

e2e: Define account boundaries for security, shared services, production, and experiments.
Choose OUs by policy requirements and document inheritance before attaching controls.
Keep workload activity out of the management account and assign administrative ownership.
Test proposed SCP effects in a limited nonproduction scope with explicit rollback access.
Monitor control status and drift, then review time-limited exceptions with accountable owners.

tasks.name: Build a small hierarchy
steps: Sketch a root with Security, Production, and Sandbox OUs, each containing fictional accounts.
Place centralized audit ownership in Security and explain why business workloads should not run in the management account.

tasks.name: Evaluate inherited constraints
steps: Assume FullAWSAccess at root and OU, an identity Allow for ec2:RunInstances, and an attached account SCP explicitly denying ec2:RunInstances.
Expected result for an affected member-account role is denied. Removing that deny only removes a limit; it does not itself grant permission. Management-account and service-linked-role cases differ.

tasks.name: Classify two controls
steps: Compare a preventive restriction on an operation with a detective check reporting noncompliant resource configuration.
Write who receives the finding and who remediates it. A dashboard entry alone is not evidence that an operation was blocked.

tasks.name: Design a safe rollout
steps: Propose one test OU, a reviewed exception, a rollback policy version, and positive and negative requests.
Explain that paper evaluation cannot prove live IAM behavior. Avoid attaching an untested deny at the organization root.

key_terms: OU: organizational unit grouping accounts for governance.
SCP: organization policy limiting affected principals.
Management account: organization administration and consolidated-billing account.
Landing zone: governed account foundation.
Detective control: mechanism identifying an undesirable state.
lesson.safety: Do not create accounts or attach policies. Account creation enables potential service spend; centralized logs and governance integrations can add costs. Broad denies can interrupt recovery operations.
cleanup: Retain the hierarchy and rollback plan.
Discard hypothetical policy drafts after review; no organization configuration changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a new root-level SCP blocks deployments in every workload account. How would you respond and prevent recurrence?
interview_points: Identify the inherited deny and affected principals.
Use approved governance recovery access rather than broad workload grants.
Roll back the reviewed policy version.
Canary future changes and maintain exception ownership.

aws-core/aws-organizations-control-tower.core: Organizations provides account hierarchy; SCPs limit affected member principals without granting access. Control Tower supports landing-zone governance but requires operational ownership. Test inherited constraints narrowly and preserve a reviewed rollback path.

storyboard.title: An inherited SCP blocks a deployment
storyboard.objective: Show organization guardrails acting before workload authorization can succeed.

scenes.title: Allowed deployment
scenes.caption: Identity grants operate inside organization limits.
scenes.narration: The deployment role can request a launch only when its grants and all applicable limits permit the operation.

scenes.title: Ancestor deny applies
scenes.caption: A local Allow cannot override this deny.
scenes.narration: A new OU policy explicitly denies launches, so the affected role's existing identity permissions cannot make the request succeed.

scenes.title: Canary the correction
scenes.caption: Restore the reviewed boundary, not unlimited access.
scenes.narration: Governance owners review and test a narrower policy version before restoring deployments and expanding the change beyond the canary.

lesson.title: AWS Systems Manager and fleet operations
lesson.why: A fleet-wide command can multiply a small mistake across every server. Systems Manager provides managed operations, but safe targeting, identity, network access, and recovery remain engineering responsibilities.
lesson.what: Plan inventory, session access, command execution, and patching for a fictional fleet. Distinguish agent connectivity and compliance reporting from actual application health.

concepts.name: A managed node needs a working path
concepts.body: SSM Agent, supported operating-system configuration, appropriate instance or managed-node permissions, and connectivity to required service endpoints enable management. Session Manager avoids needing inbound SSH for its access path, but does not automatically close existing SSH exposure or remove authorization requirements.

concepts.name: Target selection is a safety control
concepts.body: Run Command can target nodes using identifiers or tags. Tags are mutable, so previewing intended membership matters before a broad operation. Limit concurrency and errors, use a canary group, and design commands to be repeatable rather than assuming the service makes arbitrary scripts idempotent.

concepts.name: Patch compliance is policy-relative
concepts.body: Patch Manager evaluates nodes against patch baselines and can perform scanning or installation workflows. A compliant report means the baseline's requirements were met, not that every vulnerability is absent. Package availability, exclusions, reboot state, and application compatibility can alter the result.

concepts.name: Maintenance requires recovery evidence
concepts.body: Maintenance Windows schedule approved operations; Automation runbooks coordinate steps and approvals. Neither substitutes for workload backups, a tested image rollback, or post-change application checks. Command output and session records need appropriate access control and retention because they may contain sensitive operational information.

e2e: Inventory fictional nodes with owners, operating systems, criticality, and maintenance constraints.
Verify agent, permission, and endpoint prerequisites before diagnosing command delivery.
Preview a narrow canary target set and define concurrency, error, and reboot policies.
Scan first, then plan installation and application-level validation during an approved window.
Promote only after canary evidence; retain rollback instructions and bounded operational logs.

tasks.name: Find missing prerequisites
tasks.goal: Separate disconnected nodes from command failures.
steps: A node has a running agent but no route to required management endpoints; another has connectivity but lacks required permissions.
Assign network and authorization investigations respectively. Do not propose opening inbound SSH as the first Systems Manager repair.

tasks.name: Calculate rollout batches
steps: Assume 24 nodes, a two-node canary, and later batches of four with no overlapping batches.
Expected remaining batches are ceiling((24 - 2) / 4) = 6. With ten minutes per batch and ten for the canary, modeled execution is 70 minutes before extra validation or retries.

tasks.name: Interpret compliance carefully
steps: A baseline excludes a pending application-sensitive patch and the node is reported compliant.
Explain why compliance does not mean every known vulnerability is fixed; document the exception owner, expiry, reboot needs, and compensating protection.

tasks.name: Rehearse a failed canary
steps: Suppose the first patched node passes package installation but fails a synthetic application check.
Write a stop, preserve-evidence, and image-rollback sequence. These offline cases do not verify real agent behavior, cloud authorization, or patch compatibility.

key_terms: Managed node: machine configured for Systems Manager operations.
Baseline: rules defining approved patch compliance.
Canary: small initial deployment cohort.
Maintenance Window: scheduled period for operational tasks.
Idempotent command: operation safe to repeat without unintended extra effects.
lesson.safety: Do not execute fleet commands. Real operations can restart services, incur automation or logging charges, and expose secrets in output. Never include credentials in command text.
cleanup: Retain only fictional inventory and rollout decisions.
Delete scratch command drafts and note future log-retention and canary-resource cleanup responsibilities.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, patch installation succeeds on a canary but the service stops answering. What determines whether you continue?
interview_points: Treat application health as a separate release gate.
Stop remaining batches and preserve operational evidence.
Use the approved rollback and validate restored service.
Review baseline exclusions, reboot requirements, and maintenance assumptions.

aws-core/aws-systems-manager-and-fleet-o.core: Systems Manager needs agent, identity, and network prerequisites. Safe fleet operations combine previewed targets, canaries, bounded concurrency, baseline-aware compliance, and application validation. Successful command execution is not proof of service health.

storyboard.title: A patch canary stops a fleet rollout
storyboard.objective: Separate successful installation from safe application operation.

scenes.title: Patch narrowly
scenes.caption: Only the selected canary receives the change.
scenes.narration: The runbook targets a reviewed canary node, applies approved patches, and waits for independent application checks.

scenes.title: Application gate fails
scenes.caption: Installation success does not justify promotion.
scenes.narration: The package operation completes but the application fails its readiness check, so remaining fleet batches stay untouched.

scenes.title: Recover before promotion
scenes.caption: Rollback evidence controls the next decision.
scenes.narration: Operators restore the canary using the approved recovery plan and investigate compatibility before authorizing any broader patch attempt.
